Ordering and holding costs rise by £6,960 − £4,800 = £2,160, which is less than the £7,200 saving, giving a net benefit of £5,040. Delta should accept, provided it has storage space, the extra cash tied up is affordable and the component is not at risk of obsolescence. (If the holding cost depends on the price, it would fall slightly, strengthening the case.)

(c) Just-in-time, from the Toyota Production System, pulls materials only when needed, in small, frequent deliveries. Benefits include much lower inventory and holding costs, less space, faster detection of quality problems, and pressure to remove waste. However, JIT requires reliable suppliers close by, short and predictable lead times, stable demand and low ordering or set-up costs. With an ordering cost of £80, very frequent orders would be expensive unless Delta negotiates with its supplier to cut transaction costs, for example through electronic ordering or a supplier-managed arrangement.

JIT also conflicts with the bulk discount, and the fragility of lean supply chains during COVID-19 and the 2021 Suez Canal blockage shows the risk of holding no buffer. A sensible approach would be to work towards JIT with a strategic partner supplier, keep a modest safety stock, and compare the total cost of each option, including the value of resilience.

questions.q: 'Coase and Williamson explain why firms exist, but Chandler explains why they became large. Neither is sufficient alone.' Critically evaluate this statement in relation to the rise of the modern business enterprise.
markScheme: Coase (1937): transaction costs of the market explain the firm; boundary where marginal costs equal
Williamson: bounded rationality, opportunism, asset specificity; markets v hierarchies; M-form efficiency (1975)
Strengths: explains vertical integration and make-or-buy; limitations: static, efficiency-focused, neglects capabilities and power
Chandler: Strategy and Structure, Visible Hand, Scale and Scope; technology, throughput, managerial hierarchies, first-mover investments
Chandler's account explains growth and organisational innovation (railways, DuPont, GM)
Overlap: Williamson used Chandler's evidence; M-form as transaction-cost economising
Critiques of Chandler: US-centric, deterministic, neglect of networks, family firms, state and finance
Other theories: Penrose on growth, resource-based view, agency theory (Berle and Means; Jensen and Meckling)
Historical illustrations (GM–Fisher Body debate, British family capitalism)
Conclusion on complementarity and need for multiple lenses
questions.modelAnswer:
Coase (1937) asked why firms exist if markets allocate resources efficiently. His answer was that using the price mechanism has costs, such as discovering prices, negotiating and enforcing contracts, so some transactions are cheaper to organise by managerial direction. The boundary of the firm lies where the cost of organising one more transaction internally equals the cost of using the market. Williamson made this operational. Bounded rationality and opportunism make contracts incomplete, and where assets are specific to a relationship, hold-up risk favours hierarchy. This explains vertical integration, as in the classic but contested General Motors–Fisher Body case. Williamson also argued that the M-form economised on information and control costs.

Chandler's approach is historical. In The Visible Hand (1977) he showed how railways, then mass production and distribution, required managerial hierarchies to coordinate high-volume throughput, replacing market coordination. In Strategy and Structure (1962) diversification led to the M-form, and in Scale and Scope (1990) first movers who invested in production, distribution and management dominated their industries.

The statement captures a real division. Transaction cost theory is mainly static and comparative, explaining boundaries at a given moment, while Chandler explains growth driven by technology and organisational capabilities. But the division is not clean. Williamson drew heavily on Chandler's evidence, and Chandler's account of why managers replaced markets is consistent with transaction cost savings. Coase's framework also implies growth when organising costs fall, for example through telegraph and telephone.

Neither is complete. Transaction cost theory neglects capabilities, learning and power. Chandler's work has been criticised as US-centred and deterministic, undervaluing British family firms, networks and the roles of the state and finance. Other theories fill gaps: Penrose (1959) explained growth through underused managerial resources, the resource-based view emphasises capabilities, and Berle and Means and agency theory address the governance consequences of size.

Conclusion. The statement is broadly correct that the two traditions are complementary, but it understates their overlap and their shared blind spots. Explaining the modern enterprise needs economic, historical and resource-based perspectives together.

questions.q: 'The introduction of general incorporation with limited liability in mid-nineteenth-century Britain was the most important step in the development of the modern business enterprise.' Discuss.
markScheme: Before reform: chartered companies (East India Company 1600), Bubble Act 1720–1825, partnerships and unincorporated joint-stock companies
Joint Stock Companies Act 1844: registration and publicity, without limited liability
Limited Liability Act 1855 and Joint Stock Companies Act 1856; Companies Act 1862 consolidation
Effects: easier capital raising, risk-shifting, transferable shares; Salomon (1897) extended to small firms
Limits: slow uptake for manufacturing; most firms remained partnerships or private family companies; finance via retained profits and local networks
Other factors: railways, technology, managerial hierarchies (Chandler), markets and finance
Comparisons: US and Germany, where managerial capitalism grew; Chandler's critique of British personal capitalism
Reasoned conclusion: necessary but not sufficient
questions.modelAnswer:
Before the 1840s, incorporation in Britain required a royal charter or private Act of Parliament, as with the East India Company (1600). After the South Sea Bubble, the Bubble Act 1720 restricted unincorporated joint-stock companies until its repeal in 1825. Most businesses were sole traders or partnerships with unlimited liability, although canals and railways used special Acts to raise large sums.

Reform came in stages. The Joint Stock Companies Act 1844 allowed incorporation by registration and required publicity, but without limited liability. The Limited Liability Act 1855 and the Joint Stock Companies Act 1856 made limited liability generally available, and the Companies Act 1862 consolidated the law. Salomon (1897) later confirmed that even one-person businesses could use the corporate form.

The case for the statement is strong. General incorporation gave firms a separate legal identity, continuity and transferable shares, and limited liability encouraged passive investors by capping their risk. This made it possible to raise large amounts of capital from many investors and to separate ownership from management, features Berle and Means later saw as defining the modern corporation.

But the claim that it was the most important step is doubtful. Take-up in manufacturing was slow; many firms that incorporated were private companies controlled by families and financed from retained profits and local networks. Chandler argued that the defining feature of the modern enterprise was the managerial hierarchy built to coordinate mass production and distribution, made possible by railways, the telegraph and new technologies. On his account, Britain's legal head start did not prevent it from falling behind the United States and Germany, where managerial capitalism developed more fully.

Conclusion. General incorporation with limited liability was a necessary legal foundation, but not a sufficient one. Technology, markets, finance and managerial organisation determined how far firms grew, so the legal reform is better seen as an enabling condition than as the decisive step.
